articles.text: Renovation to start June 6; 400 truckloads on Palm Drive The long-delayed renovation of Witter Field’s irrigation system and turf is scheduled to begin on June 6. Work won’t be completed until approximately December 1, meaning a six month relocation of all summer and fall sports. The School District held a community meeting on Monday, May 22, with neighbors, and attended by the city’s Public Works Director. A follow-up meeting with Public Works staff on May 26 produced a construction schedule for the project. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said, “officially, the approved working hours for PUSD’s contractors during this project are 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. However, the contractors won’t be working past 4 p.m. We’ve been in discussions with the district about altering those hours to be a little earlier, while preventing significant parking burdens on local residents. We’ve also been reaching out to them about clarifying these details on their website and answering community questions in future meetings.” There will be “no parking” restrictions through the month of June, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., on Palm Drive, El Cerrito Avenue, and Winsor Avenue. According to PUSD Facilities Director Pete Palmer, the major work will be done “in June, August and September.” Witter Field at Piedmont High School.

articles.text: The city of Piedmont received additional comments on its Housing Element from the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) on May 23, as the State’s 60-day review period concluded. However, as more revisions were requested by the state, the Element is not yet state-compliant. HCD reviewers requested that the city provide additional analysis regarding housing mobility, affordability, and the likelihood of development on certain sites, along with additional details as to the timeline of implementing the Element. Planning Department staff expect to complete the requested additions and submit a revised Housing Element to HCD by mid-summer, after which another 60-day state review period will begin. If the Element is compliant by May 31, Piedmont will have three years to implement a substantial number of its programs (by January 31, 2026). But because the Element will not be compliant by May 31, the city will have less than one year to implement programs – by January 31, 2024. articles.text: Editor: The UC student presentation to the City Council on building affordable apartments in Blair Park (which is a great idea!) was good until they got to their estimate of $985,000 per unit. At that price, no apartments will ever be built, whether the land is free or paid for. Luxury apartment buildings all over the country are built for between $300,000 and $400,000 per unit and include swimming pools, spas, dog washing rooms, exercise gyms, lounges and other amenities. That $400k construction price includes land, development costs and profits of the builder and developer and all those amenities. To make a 4% return on a $400,000 unit, rent has to be at least $2,000 per month to cover property taxes, insurance and maintenance. And 4% is less than you now make in a risk-free money market fund. The student projected price of $985,000 per apartment for Blair Park shows the difference between the university world and the real world. articles.text: Earlier this month the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) launched a matching funds campaign to raise $100,000 in contributions toward landscaping to help make Piedmont’s new community pool a truly beautiful and sustainable space in the City. PBF has offered to match from its own funds all donations up to $100,000 so that $200,000 will be available to assure healthy, environmentally sound landscaping with smart irrigation to assure water conservation. From the outset of the project to build the new community pool, PBF has been a strong supporter. It endorsed Measure UU, urging voters to take the bold step of authorizing 19 million dollars to fund the building of a stateof-the-art aquatic facility. PBF was one of the first contributors to the PRFO-led effort to cover increased construction costs, pledging $25,000 to help kickstart that campaign. This new PBF campaign will support installation of native and drought-tolerant planting as well as other green infrastructure, including a solar trellis with photovoltaic cells and a bioswale for storm water retention. Descriptive brochures were recently mailed to every home in Piedmont to announce the campaign. Early returns are extremely encouraging as more than $30,000 in contributions have been received during the first few weeks. PBF President Karen Sullivan urges Piedmonters to support its effort to see that their new pool and community gathering center will be a model of sustainability, incorporating renewable energy technology, water-conserving design, and beautiful native landscaping. She emphasized that every dollar given will be doubled until together we have reached the combined total of $200,000. Contributions may be mailed to Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611. Online contributions can be sent to piedmontbeautification.org. PBF (a jointly governed organization with Trustees from the City Council and the Piedmont Garden Club, along with 25 community advisors that include representation from other local garden clubs) has been funding projects to “improve, beautify, and maintain the premises and projects of the City of Piedmont” for almost 60 years. PBF has expanded the scope of its projects to more broadly promote safety and sustainability. A separate endowment was established to help the City pay for the ever-increasing expense of maintaining its many recreational venues. Most recently, an improved entrance to Piedmont Park at the corner of Highland and Guilford will open in time for July 4th festivities. Improved lighting and handrails will enhance the safety and appeal of this access to the park and Community Hall for residents and those attending special events alike. With California wildfire season quickly approaching, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan appeared on KTVU, Channel 2 on Monday morning, May 22 to offer fire prevention and safety tips for viewers of the program. Brannigan told KTVU anchor Gasia Mikaelian that homeowners’ responsibility for fire prevention “is whatever is on your property. Cities take care of the trees and vegetation in the public rights-of-way and the parks.” Ideally, he said, people should leave at least five feet of room between vegetation and flammable property (like homes, fences and decks), and 10 feet between tree limbs and roofs or chimneys. To prevent ladder fuel – a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the landscape upward to tree or shrub canopies – Brannigan said “for the height of the fuel, you want three times the amount of space above it, so if you have one foot of grass, try to have three feet between whatever is above it.” Mikaelian suggested that property owners may find their yards in particularly dangerous situations this fire season due to high vegetation growth after last winter’s rainstorms. “We have a saying that every year is going to be the worst fire season, whether its dry and drought or whether it’s wet and a lot of growth,” Brannigan replied, urging owners to clear their yards of dead and excess vegetation ahead of the dryer months of September and October. In Piedmont particularly, he said, “We have a lot of beautiful old homes. Some have wood siding and wood shingles. Having vegetation right up against that presents a particular danger in lieu of regular tree and shrub maintenance.” In the Bay Area more broadly, he continued, “when you look at statewide [fire] guidance, it often involves five feet, thirty feet, a hundred feet, we just don’t have that kind of space, so we’re trying to come up with practical, realistic guidelines to keep your property safe as well as the adjacent properties and prevent fire from spreading.” Just as crucial a point of wildfire safety he continued, is knowledge of evacuation routes: “Know, from where you live, work, go to school, at least two ways out of your neighborhood, but also know multiple ways you can get yourself out, whether by car, by walking, whether you’re in a wheelchair or bicycle … also talk to your neighbors, if you have people around you who might need a little bit of extra help,” Brannigan said. articles.text: Assistant Piedmont High School Principal Irma Muñoz was recently named the new principal of Millennium High School. She succeeds Shannon Fierro, who will continue as Principal of Piedmont Adult School. Speaking to the Piedmont School Board on May 24, she said, “Eight years ago I joined the Piedmont community, and this moment is not only a highlight of my years in Piedmont, but of my career.” “I look forward to working with Millennium students, parents, and staff to continue its culture of support and belonging, of equity and inclusion, of seeing each student and family for the strengths and qualities that they bring to our school,” she added. “I thank you for trusting me with this important task, and I am honored to serve as the next principal of Millennium High School.” Muñoz has served as Assistant Principal at the high school since June 2015. Although The school’s other Assistant Principal, Erin Igoe, remains, and the school plans to fill Muñoz’s vacancy. Muñoz previously served as Assistant Principal at San Leandro High School from 2014 to 2015, and at Mills High School from 2006 to 2014. After graduating from UC Davis with an undergraduate degree in Chicano studies in 1995, she went on to receive master’s degrees in education from Stanford in 1996 and from UC Berkeley in 2005. She will begin doctoral studies this summer through the Leaders for Equity and Democracy program at Berkeley. Superintendent Donald Evans described more of Muñoz’s accomplishments in Piedmont beyond her administrative roles: She has been instrumental in providing mental health support for students while overseeing the PUSD Wellness Center, and has led many of the district’s Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) initiatives including the establishment of the district’s Black, Indigenous, and People of Color Network, support of Ethnic Studies and Affinity Mentorship courses, and participation on the DEIB Council,” he said. Fierro, who was appointed as principal of both MHS and Piedmont Adult School in 2017, said that she is leaving Millennium to pursue a doctoral degree in Education for Social Justice at Hayward State (CSU East Bay). Fierro will remain principal of Piedmont Adult School, and will teach 8th grade Spanish 1 at Piedmont Middle School. “I’m excited to get back into the classroom teaching world language as I did for seven years before going into administration,” she said. Irma Muñoz has been named as the new principal of Millennium High School.

articles.text: Photos by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Affinity mentor, senior Julia Banuelos, presents Sidney Dearing’s story. Piedmont High’s Associated Student Body (ASB) offered, along with the affinity mentors, a history of Piedmont presentation to all juniors and seniors in the Alan Harvey Theater on April 28. The presentation was ASB’s first large step into diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) work. The presentation educated students on Piedmont’s past with hate crimes, minstrel shows, the KKK, redlining and exclusionary housing. The story of Sidney Dearing, the first Black man to buy a home in Piedmont and who was forced to leave after numerous threats, shocked many students. While the presentation highlighted the racism of Piedmont’s past, ASB was not afraid to acknowledge the continued segregation between Piedmont and Oakland, asking students, “What is Piedmont doing that continues to create this racial divide?” ASB Junior Sara Broach worked with the class’s community outreach committee to create and present the history of Piedmont lesson. “We think that educating the student body about the history of Piedmont is important because the racist foundations our town was built on still persist today,” said Broach, “We believe that education is the first step in progressing DEI work. ASB hopes to continue integrating DEI work into our school, by supporting affinity groups, celebrating everyone’s culture, and contributing to education,” Broach added, “We know that one presentation isn’t going to fix the centuries-old issues, so we are determined to implement permanent DEI education into the school.” ASB advisor and Ethnic Studies teacher Hayley Adams finds these student assemblies necessary to confront the racism in Piedmont’s history. “This is the first time that the secondary schools have been engaged in the direct conversation of Piedmont’s racist history,” said Adams, “As the teacher of both Ethnic Studies and ASB, Juniors Elena Stevens and Jack Cramer Sara Broach and Audrey La Jeunesse offer a “South vs. Piedmont Pop Quiz.” it’s been really important to have these conversations in a larger school-wide setting.” “Ethnic Studies is much larger than it’s often perceived to be. Ethnic Studies is everything around us, everything we breathe, we do, it’s teenagers, it’s culture, it’s everything,” Adams added, “So it’s really important that ASB, is more engaged in culture.”
articles.title: PHS ASB embarks on DEI work with History of Piedmont

articles.text: Articulation errors, which affect the accurate production of speech sounds, can vary among children. I often get asked why some children effortlessly produce clear and intelligible speech, while others struggle with articulation errors. Let’s look at some of the reasons children may be difficult to understand. The most common reason for pronunciation errors is developmental. Children follow a general sequence of speech sound development based on age. As development progresses, children may temporarily make errors (usually simplifications) during certain stages. For example, children can correctly produce the “p” sound by the age of 2, whereas children may not be able to correctly produce the “r” sound until 5 or so years of age. If the errors persist beyond the age of expectancy, and/or if the child has a high number of developmental errors, we may find it quite difficult to understand the child’s message. On the other hand, differences in oral structure and function can contribute to articulation errors, instead of developmental issues. Structural abnormalities, such as cleft palate or malocclusion, can affect a child’s ability to produce specific sounds accurately. For instance, a child with a cleft palate may struggle with the production of sounds like “s” and “sh” due to the opening in the roof of their mouth. In contrast, a child without these abnormalities may have clearer speech due to the absence of physical constraints. Hearing plays a vital role in speech development. Children with hearing loss or frequent ear infections may experience difficulties perceiving and imitating Articulation errors in children are complex and influenced by a combination of factors. speech sounds accurately. For example, a child with hearing loss may produce distorted vowels because they are unable to distinguish the subtle auditory differences between vowel sounds without proper auditory input. Another possible reason for speech difficulty in children is phonological, meaning the child is having difficulty applying the rules governing sounds in English, or another language. These language specific patterns of errors affect multiple sounds. For example, by around three years of age children learning English are expected to realize that consonants are important at the end of words, for example the word “tree” vs the word “treat”, and those final consonants should be marked and change meaning. pages.text: Wednesday, May 31, 2023 9 Thinking Outside the Classroom Articulation and clear speech By Katie Pengilly Articulation errors, which affect the accurate production of speech sounds, can vary among children. I often get asked why some children effortlessly produce clear and intelligible speech, while others struggle with articulation errors. Let’s look at some of the reasons children may be difficult to understand. The most common reason for pronunciation errors is developmental. Children follow a general sequence of speech sound development based on age. As development progresses, children may temporarily make errors (usually simplifications) during certain stages. For example, children can correctly produce the “p” sound by the age of 2, whereas children may not be able to correctly produce the “r” sound until 5 or so years of age. If the errors persist beyond the age of expectancy, and/or if the child has a high number of developmental errors, we may find it quite difficult to understand the child’s message. On the other hand, differences in oral structure and function can contribute to articulation errors, instead of developmental issues. Structural abnormalities, such as cleft palate or malocclusion, can affect a child’s ability to produce specific sounds accurately. For instance, a child with a cleft palate may struggle with the production of sounds like “s” and “sh” due to the opening in the roof of their mouth. In contrast, a child without these abnormalities may have clearer speech due to the absence of physical constraints. Hearing plays a vital role in speech development. Children with hearing loss or frequent ear infections may experience difficulties perceiving and imitating Articulation errors in children are complex and influenced by a combination of factors. speech sounds accurately. For example, a child with hearing loss may produce distorted vowels because they are unable to distinguish the subtle auditory differences between vowel sounds without proper auditory input. Another possible reason for speech difficulty in children is phonological, meaning the child is having difficulty applying the rules governing sounds in English, or another language. These language specific patterns of errors affect multiple sounds. For example, by around three years of age children learning English are expected to realize that consonants are important at the end of words, for example the word “tree” vs the word “treat”, and those final consonants should be marked and change meaning. Coordination of muscle movements can also play a part in speech production for some children. For example, perhaps a child can produce all the sounds contained within a multisyllabic word in isolation or within syllables or short words, but when attempting to coordinate the movements required to put them all together in a multisyllabic word precision may be lost. Articulation errors in children are complex and influenced by a combination of factors, including developmental variations, oral structure and function, hearing impairment, and phonological skills, motor planning and coordination. Understanding these factors is essential for parents, educators, and speech-language professionals to provide appropriate support and intervention. By addressing the underlying causes of articulation errors and implementing targeted therapy strategies, children can develop clearer and more accurate speech. articles.text: The 3rd annual Day of Solidarity coalesced supportive groups within Piedmont School District for a peaceful demonstration on the third anniversary of the murder of George Floyd, May 25. An estimated 150 students, teachers, and community members met at the Exedra to show support by taking pledges of solidarity, creating signs, and discussing justice. The school event wasn’t specifically about Black Lives Matter, or LGBTQ+ solidarity, but about supporting an environment of welcoming and inclusion. “This started when a group of teachers that really cared about advancing social justice and equity in our district were hearing students say how frustrated they were and how they didn’t feel heard. We wanted to show up in a different way,” said Millennium High teacher Michelle Mazzeo, one of the event planners. One of the goals was to send a collective message about the importance of equity work in the Piedmont 5th grade students hold up their signs of solidarity at the Exedra. schools. Another part of the day was for teachers and staff to take a pledge of solidarity. Tables with pens and name tags allowed students, community members and teachers to write down their commitments on posters or to wear fun name tags on their chest. Teacher pledges this year included: “I pledge to center equity work in our schools,” and “I pledge to center students and their experiences.” One focus included protecting LGBTQ+ rights after three flags on the high school flagpole were burned, including a Pride flag, two weeks earlier. articles.text: An Olympic torch, of sorts, made its way into every 6th grade classroom on Monday May 22, signaling the commencement of the annual Greek Olympics at Witter Field. 6th graders put aside their computers and books for one morning and became athletes representing the City States of Olympia, Sparta, Athens, and Rhodes. Singing songs of their citystate, the Olympic brigade paraded from the middle school to Witter Field, where Teacher-God Hera gave a welcoming speech to the eager Piedmont Olympians. The Greek Olympics, a tradition started in 1996 by teacher Jane Hickman, serves as a culmination of the Ancient Greek studies. “Olympians, today we ask, nor, we expect you, to show us that sports unite us. May the Games be held in peace, in the true spirit of the Olympic Truce,” said school counselor Amy Sharp in the role of Hera. After the welcoming speech, each of the eight core classes performed their rehearsed chants honoring a particular God or Goddess. The Games began as groups competed in eight events. Modern changes were made: the javelin was a toilet plunger; the discus a frisbee; the shot in shot put was a softball. Longjump, tug of war, jump rope, the relay race, and the three-legged race were performed without much alteration from the Ancient Greek methods. With brightly decorated shirts representing the city states the Olympians battled for spots on the podium in each event. In lieu of being presented with medals, the top three athletes in each event received stamps on their shirts. After all events were tallied the city-state of Olympia was declared the overall winner. Olympians seeking glory were given the option of running a marathon (4 laps at Witter Field, the equivalent of one mile.) The top finishers were: 1st, Travers Kemp, 5:55 – Olympia 2nd, Olivia Nealon, 5:56 – Rhodes 3rd, Mason Gray, 5:58 – Olympia The top three runners received wreaths for their embodiment of Nike, the Goddess of Victory. An optional mile Marathon was offered after a full day of Olympic games at Witter Field. The top three 1-mile runners with newly adorned wreaths: Olivia Nealon (left), Travers Kemp and Mason Gray. Olympians in a contemporary rendition of the javelin toss with plungers. Cheers of “Sparta!” rang during the tug of war event. Rohan Sietan jumps towards the 14’ mark in the long jump. Teachers serve as the Greek pantheon and announce that Olympia was this year’s winner of the Greek Olympics. One of many relay race iterations – Piggy- back relays.

articles.text: Pied mont’s t rack team returned to Veteran’s Memorial Stadium at Buchannan High School in Clovis for the 103rd CIF State Championship meet on Friday May 26. Piedmont was represented by Parker Long in the 800 meter, and as a member of the 4x400 relay team with Christian Taylor, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, and Sam Shelby. Long finished Friday’s preliminary race in 1:55.83, placing 19th of 27 runners. He entered the race after winning the NCS Meet of Champions in 1:53.80 in his first season competing at the distance. “The top people were going to be around 1:51, so I knew I had my work cut out for me in a really tight field. I feel like I’m learning more about every position in the 800; where’s it’s good to be, where it isn’t good to be, and when to kick and make your move. I feel like I’m understanding the event more,” described Long. Piedmont lacrosse stars Jack Nelson and Molly Ashton were named as the school’s 2023 Outstanding Senior Athletes, an honor that includes academics, student leadership, and citizenship. articles.text: The Spring season of the Piedmont Junior Running Club program for 4th and 5th graders concluded with a mini-track meet on Wednesday, May 24, at Witter Field.. A total of 60 boys and girls from Beach, Havens, and Wildwood Elementary Schools participated, with four running events and one field event. The Junior Running Club, created by Leonard Goldman, provides an introduction to running for kids not yet in middle school, and every season concludes with a track meet. This year’s meet included a 75-yard sprint, 60-yard hurdles Photos by Steve Zirklebach Nicholas Phung, Graham Grippando, Eleanor Chi, and Trina Branneria in the 75-yard sprint Charley Harnett, Finley Muthig, Evan Jahn, Eleanor Hathorn, and Liliane Giguere in the 60-yard hurdles 5th graders Bailey Gregovich, Simone Tornatore, Kenji Holt, and Miles Duran Xuan Tran, Miles Duran, Finley Muthig, Henley Azad, Sofia Faucher, and Teo Wickner in the sprint Runners in the 4x100m Relay 5th grade long jumper Ben Cole Half milers Saya Presley, Ronan Price, Noah Adams, and Kai Synder in the 800-meter run race, 800-meter run, 4x100-meter relay, and long jump. There were eight heats in the sprints with the Graham Grippando, Siena Botero, Theo Thomas, Sammy Laubach, and Eli Song in the 60-yard hurdles Distance runners Kenji Holt and Trina Branneria Kian Ghassemi, Harriet Killion, Sammy Laubach, Solomon Sandrock, and Kai Synder in the 800-meter run Willa Brozowski-Schrader and Teak Hergott in the 800-meter run winners advancing to the finals. The same format applied to the hurdles using three 12-inch hurdles and one 6-inch hurdle in each lane. The winner of both the sprint and hurdles was Henley Azad a 5th grader at Havens. Her time in the sprint was 10.9 seconds and 9.15 seconds in the hurdles. Teams of four runners from each school participated in the relays, with each running a 100- meter leg. There were two heats, and a team from Havens won the first heat in 66.6 seconds, a new record in the event. The winner of heat two and 2nd place overall winner was a team from Beach in a time of 68.8 seconds. The concluding running event was 800 meters (the equivalent of a half mile). Wildwood 5th grader Kenji Holt won the first heat with a time of 2-minutes, 46-seconds. The winner of heat two was Azad in a time of 2:57. The May 24 meet was the last sports event at Witter Field before it is closed for nearly six months for a renovation of the field and track. The Piedmont Junior Running Club is a year-round running program for kids in grades 2-5. It will hold a four-week summer program starting in July, followed by a Fall program that begins when school is back in session. For more information, contact Len Goldman at lgoldman@pacbell.net.

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is currently showing an exhibit by Frank Bowling titled Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966–1975, It is the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in 40 years. Sir Richard Sheridan Patrick Michael Aloysius Franklin Bowling, known as Frank Bowling, was born in British Guiana, now Guyana, and moved from London to New York. He is best known for his large-scale, abstract and colorful paintings, color field painting and lyrical abstraction; sometimes referred to as ‘abstract expressionism.’ The San Francisco exhibition features 45 vibrant and large-scale paintings, and a selection of archival materials, including recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, and film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. “We are looking forward to engaging our communities with the exceptional work of Frank Elder Sun Benjamin, 2018, by Frank Bowling Bowling and to offering an in-depth exploration of the enduring influence of his time in New York, both on his own work and on the development of art more broadly,” said Christopher Bedford, the Director at SFMOMA. “In particular, the presentation of the exhibition provides an opportunity to experience Bowling as a scholar and teacher committed to elevating the voices of Black artists and expanding the understanding of art history as it unfolded. This very much aligns with our institutional vision to share significant, if perhaps lesser-known, facets of artists’ careers and to explore artistic achievement through a spectrum of lenses and perspectives.” Frank Bowling – The New York Years opened May 20, and will be on display through September 10. The exhibition is co-organized with the Museum of Fine Arts Boston. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit www.sfmoma.org.

It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “Few may be aware of the distinctive art and visual propaganda that was central to the splendor and drama of the Tudor court,” said Thomas P. articles.text: I acknowledge that Kidnap is pulp cinema. A B-movie which has an A-list, Oscar-winning actress handling just about every moment of this unpretentious thriller. It is quite a ride. Here’s the set up: Karla Dyson (Halle Berry) is a waitress and a devoted single mom. Her sweet 6-year-old son is Frankie (Sage Correa), who is sitting at the restaurant counter coloring, waiting for his mom to get off work. Finally they leave and head for an afternoon at the park, replete with lots of fun stuff for kids. Clearly Karla is a committed mom who adores her small boy. While they are sitting trying to decide what to do next, she gets a phone call on her cell from her divorce lawyer. Concerned, she tells Frankie to sit in his chair, not to move, and then turns away, walks several steps up a hill, and has a disconcerting conversation about custody. She breaks the conversation and says, “Marco…” and waits for “Polo.” Hearing Frankie’s response she ends the conversation and returns to her seat; however, when she gets there, Frankie is gone. Missing. Frantic, she begins calling out “Marco” but gets no “Polo” in reply. Hurrying through the park she calls out to the boy. Nothing. And then she sees a large, wild-haired woman pushing Frankie into the backseat of a blue Mustang. Screaming she runs after the car and helplessly watches it speed away. It’s at this point that Kidnap becomes a pure adrenalin-inducing movie. Karla doesn’t wait for the police to arrive; she doesn’t look to others in the park for help, though there are other mothers who are concerned. articles.text: Aaron Sorkin, the gifted screenwriter who wrote Steve Jobs and The Social Network, as well as countless installments of The West Wing, is known for his rapid and succinct dialogue. He is a master of language, especially when spoken by bright, erudite characters. The film Steve Jobs is a valentine to those scenes om which people are confined to rooms while engaged in thrust and parry conversations. The question, however, is does a filmgoer, no matter the superb writing, want to spend two hours with an individual who is a driven, arrogant, manipulative, hubristic jerk? Sorkin took a great deal of literary license with Jobs as a man and with what is considered to be the definitive biography written by Walter Isaacson. This is not a biopic but an impressionistic canvas upon which the filmmaker creates a man who, while familiar, may be unrecognizable to those who actually knew him. What Sorkin and director Danny Boyle (Slumdog Millionaire) do is create three acts that are perfectly balanced. Act one involves the introduction of the Macintosh computer in 1984; act two is Jobs, now fired from Apple, introduces a computer known as NEXT in 1988; and act three is about the 1998 launch of the iMac. As each computer is brought forward, sitting stage center in a huge auditorium filled with enthuMichael Fassbender protrays Steve Jobs in Steve Jobs siastic believers, there is tension and drama backstage. Friends, colleagues and family show up just before Jobs walks out on that stage and all the current and prior issues in his life are confronted. During his pre-launch moments, the character of Jobs is revealed, each encounter a window into his persona: he is abusive, aspirational, visionary and dictatorial. In many ways Steve Jobs is a forensic examination of a man and his baggage. He was adopted as a baby, his biological parents relinquishing him, something that John Sculley (Jeff Daniels) discusses with Jobs in an attempt to push him toward self-understanding, hoping to give him insights into his inner demons, But it was impossible for Jobs – too bright and armored. The film is also a morality tale, predicated on the assumption that there can exist in the same individual two people who do battle with one another: the genius who is obsessive and driven as well as that person who can briefly drop his defenses and yield. Ever so slightly. Jobs believed he was going to change the world. And in truth he did. Millions of people now stand, heads bent downward, focused on screens, believing they are connected. He did this not as an engineer or coder, which he was not, but as someone who could see the revolutionary potential computers possessed. He tells Lisa that she will soon carry a thousand songs in her pocket and not on a Walkman brick. The film is a buffet of superb acting, led by Michael Fassbender as Jobs. His portrayal is complemented at every turn by Kate Winslet as his loyal marketing manager, Joanna Hoffman. Jeff Daniels is spot-on as the laconic Sculley, as is Seth Rogen in the role of the decent Steven “Woz” Wozniak. This film asks to be admired while also creating feelings of ambivalence. Steve Jobs. Directed by Danny Boyle. Starring Michael Fassbender, Kate Winslet, Seth Rogen. 2 hrs. Rated R. Perhaps it’s as simple as Harry possessing a magical power and an abiding fearlessness, something that every young person would delight in having. To write and direct a film that captures the essence of being 17, when your life feels unmoored and uncertain, that is no small thing. Director Kelly Fremon Craig gets it just right, avoiding clichés. At the center is Nadine (Hailee Steinfeld), suffering a perfect storm of emotions. Several years ago she lost her father, to whom she was especially close. And now her best friend since childhood, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has fallen for her older, eternally perfect and popular brother, Darian (Blake Jenner). Nadine feels abruptly rejected and betrayed and so banishes Krista from her life. Convinced she is utterly alone, she decides to kill herself. During lunch hour she informs her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (played wonderfully by Woody Harrelson) of her intention. While Nadine is a master of histrionics and self-absorbed drama, the laconic and dry Mr. Bruner becomes the perfect counterweight to her mood swings. Their classroom scenes are some of the best in the film. Meanwhile, Nadine fantasizes in a lustful way about Nick (Alexander Calvert), a bad boy, edgy, enigmatic, who works part time at Pet Land. Nadine also finds herself drawn to a classmate, Erwin (Hayden Szeto), a budding filmmaker and gifted illustrator. The Edge of Seventeen is not a collage of adolescent stereotypes; rather, it’s a film about fully formed characters. articles.text: As you probably know, Napa Valley has specific geographic parameters that are set by U.S. law. Within the Napa AVA (American Viticultural Area) there are 16 separate smaller subAVA’s that give more specificity to where the grapes on the label come from. articles.text: An early 20th century look at Piedmont Park When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had two destinations for their weekly walk last on May 24. They were aware of the recent assaults of older adults, and they wanted to attend a public meeting on safety by Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. They decided to take a short walk to Sierra, Caperton, and Guilford Avenues and be back at the Community Hall by 11:15 for Bowers’ talk. Milt Edelin and his wife, Yvonne, who live on Sierra, offered to have the group visit their gardens. The group could also get a peek of a special room in their house based on the design in Marie Antoinette’s Le Petit Trianon outside of Paris, and it was added to their house in the 1920s. As the group made its way on Sierra, the walkers noted the street’s lovely homes, some of which were designed by Julia Morgan in the early 20th Century. Milt and Yvonne took the walkers up their driveway past the front yard garden to more flowers along the house’s side and back. They peeked into the house and saw a room that is a recreation of French history. Marie Antoinette would feel at home in the beautiful sitting room with its amazing ceiling. The walkers then walked Caperton and Guilford Avenues to the Community Hall for the safety presentation. The hall was quickly filling and soon more than 100 people were ready for the safety discussion. Seniors group leader Janet Epstein welcomed everyone and introduced Chief Bowers. He provided information on the recent Piedmont robberies, and described how surveillance cameras and the city’s car license plate readers are powerful tools. He described his officers’ response to the crimes and complimented the Oakland Police Department for their work. He said he and his officers take what happened in the city personally, and he wanted residents to know Piedmont Police will respond to their calls and protect them. He said we cannot let what happened keep us from living our lives, but we can take precautions. People should be aware of the time of day, consider the routes they are taking, and let people know where they are going. If confronted, people should give up possessions and extricate themselves for the situations as quickly as possible. Catalytic converter thieves are a big problem now, and they carry weapons. People should not confront them, but rather call the police. Chief Bowers also said more license plate readers are coming to Piedmont, and he is creating a “Cop on the Block” program with officers, including himself, walking all of Piedmont streets. He also introduced Commander Lisa Douglas, who heads PPD’s dispatch center. She also provided helpful information on how to best call in issues. Many attendee questions were then taken. Everyone agreed it was an excellent, informative discussion. The walkers appreciated Janet Epstein and the Seniors group for scheduling it, and the great work Chief Bowers and his team are doing. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Walkers attend public safety meeting By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group had two destinations for their weekly walk last on May 24. They were aware of the recent assaults of older adults, and they wanted to attend a public meeting on safety by Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. They decided to take a short walk to Sierra, Caperton, and Guilford Avenues and be back at the Community Hall by 11:15 for Bowers’ talk. Milt Edelin and his wife, Yvonne, who live on Sierra, offered to have the group visit their gardens. The group could also get a peek of a special room in their house based on the design in Marie Antoinette’s Le Petit Trianon outside of Paris, and it was added to their house in the 1920s. As the group made its way on Sierra, the walkers noted the street’s lovely homes, some of which were designed by Julia Morgan in the early 20th Century. Milt and Yvonne took the walkers up their driveway past the front yard garden to more flowers along the house’s side and back. They peeked into the house and saw a room that is a recreation of French history. Marie Antoinette would feel at home in the beautiful sitting room with its amazing ceiling. The walkers then walked Caperton and Guilford Avenues to the Community Hall for the safety presentation. The hall was quickly filling and soon more than 100 people were ready for the safety discussion. Seniors group leader Janet Epstein welcomed everyone and introduced Chief Bowers. He provided information on the recent Piedmont robberies, and described how surveillance cameras and the city’s car license plate readers are powerful tools. He described his officers’ response to the crimes and complimented the Oakland Police Department for their work. He said he and his officers take what happened in the city personally, and he wanted residents to know Piedmont Police will respond to their calls and protect them. He said we cannot let what happened keep us from living our lives, but we can take precautions. People should be aware of the time of day, consider the routes they are taking, and let people know where they are going. If confronted, people should give up possessions and extricate themselves for the situations as quickly as possible. Catalytic converter thieves are a big problem now, and they carry weapons. People should not confront them, but rather call the police. Chief Bowers also said more license plate readers are coming to Piedmont, and he is creating a “Cop on the Block” program with officers, including himself, walking all of Piedmont streets. He also introduced Commander Lisa Douglas, who heads PPD’s dispatch center. She also provided helpful information on how to best call in issues. Many attendee questions were then taken. Everyone agreed it was an excellent, informative discussion. The walkers appreciated Janet Epstein and the Seniors group for scheduling it, and the great work Chief Bowers and his team are doing. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. articles.text: An energetic group of 16 members of the Piedmont Seniors traveled to the Peninsula on May 11 for a visit to the Pulgas Water Temple, and Filoli Gardens. The Water Temple is a monument to the engineering marvel that brought water from Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct, which supplies water to San Francisco and the Peninsula. This is a charming park that looks like a scene from a movie, with a reflection pool lined with cypress trees and a dome with marble columns. It is a hidden gem that is close to neighboring Peninsula towns. This oasis is a wonderful spot for wedding ceremonies, as well as a relaxing place to have a picnic or simply relax. The Pulgas Water Temple was only a half mile from the Seniors’ next stop, the majestic Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside. William Bourn, Filoli’s first owner, created the motto: “Fight for a just cause, love your fellow man, live a good life”. Thus, the term ‘Filoli’ was established (Fi for Fight; lo for love; li for life). Mr. Bourn’s major source of income was the Empire Gold Mine. The Piedmont Seniors spent much of the day exploring the 16 acres of formal gardens, along with a stop at the Visitors Center, the Rose Garden, Pool pavilion, and Courtyard. After the 1906 earthquake, wealthy Californians sought an escape from the earthquake and fire ravaged city of San Francisco. The second owners of Filoli, the Roth family, purchased the property in 1937 and were known for lavish parties, After Mr. Roth’s death, his wife donated the house and gardens to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, believing that “Filoli is too beautiful to be private”. The house is worth visiting on its own merit. It is composed of 54,256 square feet with 56 rooms, 10 main bedrooms, 14 staff bedrooms, 15 bathrooms and 17 fireplaces! The house took three years Piedmont Seniors at the Pulgas Water Temple in Redwood City. Pictured are (front): Madeline Moore (left), Elene Manolis, Nancy Hinsch, Larry and Tanya Hu, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Sue Getreuer; (back) Jim Ayotte, Ann Morales, Shelley Stafford, Fred Pemberton, and Gregory Jurin. Not pictured: Mona Jamieson, Irene Westler and Yorkman Lowe. to build and cost $425,000, which would be $8.5 million in 2020, a price that doesn’t include the Gardens and auxiliary buildings. The Seniors spent some time ogling the 1896 Tiffany sterling silver service for 18, housed in a custom-made chest. It was wheeled into the dining room for special occasions. The Reception Room was the main entertaining space at Filoli. Both the Bourn and the Roth families greeted guests and hosted large parties there. Located directly by the main entrance, it is open and spacious, reminiscent of the great halls of English country estates. The kitchen was used for the preparation of all food for the family, guests, and staff. At times, as many as nine meals were prepared each day, for family and staff. Filoli is a pleasant, serene place where visitors can enjoy a relaxing lunch. The Quail’s Nest Café, with both indoor and outdoor seating, can be a busy place to have a meal. Each season has its own unique beauty; in the Spring, multitudes of flowers are in bloom. The Seniors learned that during Mother’s Day weekend, there were 3,500 visitors a day – its busiest time of the year. During the Christmas holidays, the mansion is elegantly decorated with many trees, holly, and beautiful flower arrangements, along with a boutique. Before leaving, the Seniors couldn’t pass up a visit to the Clock Tower Gift Shop, which contains unique items for gifts and souvenirs. This excursion proved to be one of the most enjoyable outings in recent years. About Piedmont Seniors For more information on the Piedmont Seniors activities and meetings, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The group always welcomes new members. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to partake in their activities. Monthly meetings are on the fourth Wednesday of the month at 11 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall The Piedmont Seniors group in front of Filoli Home Museum in Redwood City.

By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I just upgraded my iPhone to the latest software, and it seems that my battery life has really gone down. The phone is less than a year old, so I don’t understand why it goes down so fast. Do you have any advice? Bradford K., Piedmont Dear Bradford: It’s not unusual for the battery to be drained for a while during an operating system update, just like on your computer, Spotlight on your iPhone has to re-index after an update. And the more things like photos, notes, email you have on your phone, the longer this can take. There are also processes that help the update be completed and this can be a battery drain for a while. It should even out eventually. But it’s wise to make sure that some settings you have aren’t causing unnecessary drain on your iPhone battery. 1. Check which apps are using a high percentage: Go to Settings/Battery/ and scroll down to see which apps are using the most battery. Also, while you are there, check Battery Health & Charging to make sure your battery capacity is still operating well relative to when it was new. If the capacity is less than 80%, it may be time to get a new phone or battery. 2. Go to Settings/ Display & Brightness (or swipe down diagonally from right to left to bring up the control center) and turn your brightness down. Operating at full brightness can really eat up your battery. 3. Turn off Raise to Wake, also in Settings/ Display & Brightness, and make sure the Raise to Wake button is off (gray). While you are there, make sure Auto lock is set to a reasonable time (2 or 3 minutes). Shorter time is best for battery health. 4. Turn on Auto Brightness. This setting adjusts your screen brightness according to the levels of ambient light. To do this go to: Settings/Accessibility/ Display and Text Size and scroll to the bottom, and switch on Auto-Brightness. 5. Turn off Background App Refresh: Go to Settings/General/ Background App Refresh and toggle it off. This means apps will not refresh until you turn them on, and most of the time you won’t even notice a difference, except you will notice better battery performance. 6. Use Low Power Mode. This is useful if you were running out of battery in a place where you don’t have a charging station. It’s suspense background activity and other processes on the phone to help extend battery life. To enable this, go to: Settings/Battery /Low Power Mode. 7. Turn off keyboard haptics. Anything that makes the phone vibrate, including keyboard, haptics, can drain the battery. To disable this, go to Settings/Sounds & Haptics and make sure Keyboard Feedback is set to “None”. Unless you need to have a vibration during ring or silent mode, you can turn those features off here, too. 8. Set your mail to “Fetch” and not “Push”. If you have your mail set to “Push”, your iPhone will automatically retrieve mail as it comes into your mail server. But if you send it to “Fetch”, it will come in when you determine, either every 15, 30, 60 minutes, or manually. Set it less frequently to help with battery performance. This can be done per account, so, for example, if you’re waiting for a very important email from one of your email accounts, you can have a more active setting for that account. 9. Turn off location services for apps that don’t need it (which in reality is most of them). Go to Settings/Privacy and Security/ Location Services. Some things like airline apps can be set to “While Using” and others can be set to “Never”. 10. Turn off some of the System Services. Go to Settings/ Privacy&Security/Location Services/System Services. Scroll to the bottom and turn off iPhone analytics, routing in traffic, and improve maps in product improvement. Also, you can turn off most of the system services except may be emergency calls, and SOS, find my iPhone, and may be setting time zone if you’re traveling. 11. Force restart your phone: sometimes a force restart can help solve battery issues. You can force restart any modern iPhone with Face ID by pressing Volume Up, then pressing Volume Down, then pressing and holding the Side/Power button until you see the Apple logo on screen. If none of these seem to help, it may be time to schedule an appointment with Apple to make sure there is nothing wrong with the actual hardware. articles.text: Why it matters as a grandmother, grandfather The term Grandparent conjures up all kinds of images. When you imagine yourself in the role, what do you see? It might surprise you to know that the kind of grandparent you are is likely to reflect the kind of parent you have been over the years. What kind of parent-child relationship have you had with your child? Do you fit into one of these categories? • The Expert You are a guiding light in your child’s life and they seem to forever be turning to you for advice on every single issue that arises. Making decisions on their own is still a work in progress and they always want to run things by you first. • The Tyrant You make all the decisions. It has been difficult for you as your kids have grown into adults and strive for independence. You know they aren’t mature enough to make big decisions, and you wield your power in most matters. • The Old-Timer Your kids have always thought that your opinions and advice are completely outdated and that you’re just not in tune with the world. They think you’re adorable. Every time you open your mouth, your children giggle about your vocabulary, your lack of tech savvy, and your old-fashioned ideas. • The Worrier Your children are constantly reassuring you that Everything is ok, This is normal, We’ve got this. They get exasperated with you because they can’t seem to take a step without your habit of pointing out the (non-existent) dangers that lurk around every corner. • The Playmate Everyone in the family knows you are the fun one. Kids and animals are always drawn to you, yet you don’t know the first thing about child safety, health, discipline, or nutrition, and you don’t care! You’re wonderful, but unreliable. • The Workhorse You do it all–shopping, cooking, cleaning, car-pooling, planning–and you fit everything into your day, no matter what, even though you have always held a full-time job. You never say no to anything your child needs from you or asks you to do. • The Nurturer You see things through your kids’ eyes, and help them be their best self. Your children look to you for guidance, but they know you will always allow them to make their own choices in life. You are an active listener, and gentle and sensitive with your opinions. You are cheering for them at every success and hug them close when they are in distress. These are just a few examples of the many categories of parent-child dynamics that can evolve in a family, and of course there’s lots of overlap. What’s helpful to recognize is that your family’s history of interaction will influence how you relate to each other once your child becomes a parent. What could possibly go wrong? The Expert may find that they are not knowledgeable enough on some topics to be helpful. The Tyrant may find it difficult to be cut out of decision making. The Old-Timer may always feel they are an outsider in a modern family. The Worrier might require an unreasonable amount of reassurance about raising a child today. The Playmate may be useless as a caregiver. The Workhorse could be crushed under responsibilities that they can’t handle and don’t know how to escape. Be The Nurturer. As a nurturing grandparent, you are building upon the relationship of mutual respect that you started when you were a young parent. When your kids were small you taught them good manners, and helped them develop compassion and empathy for others. You asked their opinion often and allowed them to make their own choices as long as they were safe ones. You helped them to understand that they are not the only person in the world, and encouraged them to care about other people’s feelings. You celebrated their successes and were a safety net for them when they needed one. You were, and still are, a role model for them. Take the first step towards self-awareness and think about how your parenting personality may now influence your grandparenting style. If you need to make a few changes, try and do that. Prioritize your relationship with your adult children. When that relationship is strong and mutually respectful, the joyous and loving relationship with your grandchildren can flourish. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. articles.text: Clive Chandler, 87, passed away at Alta Bates Hospital on May 25, 2023, after a brief illness. Clive grew up on Hunts Point in Bellevue, Washington, the son of Marshall and Helen (Beer) Chandler. He attended Lakeside Academy in Seattle and Phillips Academy in Andover, Massachusetts, graduating from Andover in 1953. He went on to Princeton University, studying international politics and economics at the Woodrow Wilson School, and graduated cum laude four years later. In 1968 he obtained a law degree magna cum laude from Georgetown University School of Law. Clive entered the U.S. Foreign Service after college graduation as the youngest foreign service officer in the history of the American foreign service. He was 21 years, two months old. He served in the Mediterranean area – Naples, Italy; Nice, France; and Algiers, Algeria, interspersed by assignments in Washington, D.C. and with the U.S. Mission to the United Nations. As personal aide to the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations in 1959-1960, Clive witnessed the chaotic UN session where Nikita Khrushchev, Fidel Castro, Gamal Abdel Nasser, Harold Macmillan and other world leaders delivered their demands and Khrushchev famously banged his shoe. The Algiers stint was marked by the French-Algerian war in which the Arab population rebelled and the indigenous French people of Algeria, led by the Secret Army Organization, fought a terrorist resistance against both the Arab rebels and the French Government, leading to the independence of Algeria in 1962. In Washington, as a sidelight to his normal duties, Clive was a French-English, English-French interpreter for a variety of American personalities, including the U.S. President, Vice President, Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense, and was one of the interpreters on the day of the burial of President Kennedy. In 1968, having earned a law degree through Georgetown University’s four-year night program, Clive left the Foreign Service, and moved to New York City as an associate at the Dewey Ballantine law firm. That year, he and Margaret Ann Eliel married in her hometown, Alexandria, Virginia. Four years later, they and their newly-born daughter, Margaret, moved to Beach Camp on the south coast of Trinidad in the West Indies. They lived there for six years while Clive worked as Administrative Manager and Legal Adviser to Trinidad-Tesoro Petroleum Company Limited, a 51-49 joint venture of Trinidad and Tobago and Tesoro Petroleum. Their son, Ted, was born in 1974. Clive considered the multicultural, multiracial atmosphere of Trinidad an excellent setting for his young family and they all have fond memories of those years. In 1978, Clive was asked to become Vice President and General Counsel of Tesoro in San Antonio, Texas, but he declined in favor of Buttes Gas & Oil Co., a much smaller New York Stock Exchange petroleum company. It was based in Oakland and allowed him to be closer to his family on the West Coast. He helped Buttes reorganize financially, and in 1986 he moved to the legal department of Bechtel Corporation in San Francisco. Clive greatly enjoyed legal and petroleum work and had some notable successes: delivering ground-breaking interpretations of the U. S.-Trinidad and Tobago double-tax treaty, negotiating a favorable outcome of Buttes’s dispute with the National Iranian Oil Company over petroleum deposits in the Strait of Hormuz of the Persian Gulf, and drafting a new petroleum policy, law and regulations for Romania after the fall of the Soviet empire. He continued to work long after normal retirement age. Clive and Ann and their two children moved to Piedmont in 1978 and became members of Clive and Ann Chandler celebrate their honeymoon on Guadeloupe in 1969. Clive Chandler, a member of the U.S. Foreign Service for 20 years and a Piedmont resident since 1978, died on May 25. He was 87. Piedmont Community Church. His community involvement included helping found the Piedmont Choirs (now the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs) and volunteering on the board of the Piedmont Swim Club (now the Piedmont Community Pool). He is remembered by many Piedmont parents and children as the host of a summer retreat at Pope Valley where many Piedmont children learned to swim, fish and drive an automobile at a sprawling vineyard property of several thousand acres. He was a caring and supportive husband and father, and was particularly pleased that both his daughter and son graduated from Princeton University, his alma mater. Clive is predeceased by his parents and by his sister, Marcia Johnson. He is survived by his wife of 54 years, Ann; his daughter and son-in-law Margaret and Jeff Hiller of Piedmont, and son and daughter-in-law, Ted and Giselle Chandler of Santa Monica. He is survived by grandchildren Megan and Genevieve Hiller of Piedmont, and Layla and Roya Chandler of Santa Monica. He is also survived by his sister and brother-in-law, Henrietta and Jim Ratcliff of Oakland, and five nieces and nephews and their families. Private graveside services were held recently in Mountain View Cemetery. The family requests that in lieu of flowers, memorial donations be made to the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs, the Piedmont Community Church, or a charity of your choice. The Chandler family 50 years after Clive and Ann Chandler were married. Pictured are Genevieve, Megan, Jeff and Margaret Hiller (left), Clive and Ann Chandler, Ted, Giselle and Layla Chandler with infant Roya in 2019.

Perhaps what is most famous and architecturally notable in Portugal is the iconic glazed ceramic tile seen everywhere – on walls, floors, ceilings, and fountains. Moorish in origin, they were apparently first imported via Spain, after which Lisbon created its own tile industry. Called azulejos (“polished stone” in Arabic), in the beginning they were individual patterned tiles, mostly blue, yellow, green and white, but Not all new building is great or even good. Clearly aesthetically lacking, the visually overpowering continuous balconies are an unfortunate common architectural style seen all over the world. Something for us to remember to avoid on our own new projects. Faberman Memorial Prize – Aryana Fisher Piedmont senior Aryana Fisher was named the recipient of the annual Dean Faberman Memorial Prize. The plaque is awarded to a graduating senior who excels in public speaking and debate. While attending UC Berkeley, Dean Faberman was killed by a drunk driver. The prize was created by the Faberman family to remind others of the inherent risks of drinking and driving. Faberman, a 1979 Piedmont High graduate, excelled in public speaking. This year’s winner of the award, Aryana Fisher, was a member the PHS Mock Trial team for four years, serving as co-captain her junior year and president her senior year. Former Mock Trial coach Dave Keller said her confidence and professional demeanor in front of coaches and court officials is unparalleled. Fisher took over many coaching responsibilities when Keller had to step back from the role in 2021. She dedicated a tremendous amount of time to mentor her teammates, ultimately guiding them to two consecutive semifinal placements. Fisher was awarded the 1st Place Outstanding Prosecuting Attorney Award in 2022 and the Competitor of the Year Award in 2023 by the Alameda County Office of Education for her performances in the Phillip A.
